claim: Platynereis nectochaete larvae have segmentally arranged locomotor ciliated cells that form distinct ciliated fields.
source: Platynereis nectochaete larvae have segmentally arranged locomotor ciliated cells that form distinct ciliated fields (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by scanning electron micrographs and serial TEM reconstruction shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: The main ciliary band (prototroch) is located between the head and the trunk.
source: The main ciliary band (prototroch) is located between the head and the trunk.
evidence: Supported by anatomical description and imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: The head has two patches of locomotor cilia (akrotroch).
source: The head has two patches of locomotor cilia (akrotroch) and multiciliated cells that cover the olfactory pit of the nuchal organs (nuchal cilia).
evidence: Supported by anatomical description and imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: There is an unpaired multiciliated cell, the crescent cell, located anteriorly in the head in the middle of the sensory region of the apical organ.
source: There is also an unpaired multiciliated cell, the crescent cell, located anteriorly in the head in the middle of the sensory region of the apical organ.
evidence: Supported by anatomical description and imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: The three chaetigerous trunk segments each have four fields of cilia forming the paratroch ciliary bands (paratroch I-III).
source: The three chaetigerous (with chaetae) trunk segments each have four fields of cilia forming the paratroch ciliary bands (paratroch I-III).
evidence: Supported by anatomical description and imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: There is an additional non-chaetigerous cryptic segment between the head and the trunk segments that harbours ventrally the metatroch ciliary band.
source: There is an additional non-chaetigerous cryptic segment between the head and the trunk segments (Steinmetz et al., 2011) that harbours ventrally the metatroch ciliary band.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and anatomical description.

claim: Younger larvae have four posterior telotroch cells that merge with the paratroch III during development to form a posterior ciliary band of 12 cells.
source: Younger larvae have four posterior telotroch cells that merge with the paratroch III (eight cells) during development to form a posterior ciliary band of 12 cells (Starunov et al., 2015) (referred to as paratroch III).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work describing developmental changes.

claim: Spontaneous arrests of ciliary beating occurred synchronously across all ciliary bands.
source: We found that spontaneous arrests of ciliary beating occurred synchronously across all ciliary bands (Figure 1A–E and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing synchronized ciliary arrests across different ciliary bands.

claim: Cilia first resumed beating in the prototroch followed in synchrony by the paratroch cilia with a delay of 19 ± 3 msec relative to the prototroch cilia.
source: Cilia first resumed beating in the prototroch followed in synchrony by the paratroch cilia (with a delay of 19 ± 3 msec relative to the prototroch cilia).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements from imaging experiments.

claim: Arrests of prototroch cilia were in synchrony with arrests in the akrotroch.
source: Arrests of prototroch cilia were also in synchrony with arrests in the akrotroch (Video 2) and the nuchal cilia (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by video imaging data showing synchronized arrests.

claim: Regular arrests are triggered by bursts of spikes that can be recorded from the ciliary band cells.
source: In Platynereis larvae, regular arrests are triggered by bursts of spikes that can be recorded from the ciliary band cells (Conzelmann et al., 2011; Tosches et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: Periodic synchronous increases in calcium signals in cells of each ciliary band corresponded with the arrests of cilia.
source: With calcium imaging, we detected periodic synchronous increases in calcium signals in cells of each ciliary band that corresponded with the arrests of cilia (Figure 1G, Video 3).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments showing correlation between calcium signals and ciliary arrests.

claim: The cilia of the crescent cell did not beat and arrest synchronously with other locomotor cilia.
source: The only cilia that did not beat and arrest synchronously were the cilia of the crescent cell (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing distinct behavior of crescent cell cilia.

claim: Calcium signals increase in the crescent cell simultaneously with the other multiciliated cells.
source: Although calcium signals also increase in the crescent cell simultaneously with the other multiciliated cells (data not shown), the cilia of this cell were beating when the other cilia were arrested (Video 2).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing simultaneous calcium increases.

claim: Crescent cilia stopped beating after the locomotor cilia resumed beating.
source: Crescent cilia stopped beating after the locomotor cilia resumed beating (Video 2).
evidence: Supported by video imaging data showing temporal relationship of crescent cilia beating.

claim: The crescent cell has a lower density of cilia that beat more irregularly and do not organise into metachronal waves.
source: The crescent cell has a lower density of cilia that beat more irregularly and do not organise into metachronal waves (Video 2 and Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing structural and functional differences of crescent cell cilia.

claim: Ciliary activity did not correlate with the absolute levels of intracellular calcium concentration, but with the time derivative of calcium d[Ca2+]i/dt.
source: We found that ciliary activity did not correlate with the absolute levels of [Ca2+]i, but with the time derivative of calcium d[Ca2+]i/dt (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by high frame rate calcium imaging analysis showing correlation with calcium derivative.

claim: As long as calcium levels increase, the cilia are arrested.
source: As long as calcium levels increase, the cilia are arrested.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing relationship between calcium dynamics and ciliary state.

claim: As soon as calcium levels start to drop, the cilia resume their metachronal beating.
source: As soon as calcium levels start to drop, the cilia resume their metachronal beating.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing relationship between calcium dynamics and ciliary state.

claim: In sea urchin sperm, d[Ca2+]i/dt rather than absolute [Ca2+]i controls ciliary waveform during chemotaxis.
source: A similar case was reported in sea urchin sperm where d[Ca2+]i/dt rather than absolute [Ca2+]i controls ciliary waveform during chemotaxis (Alvarez et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on sea urchin sperm.

claim: There are 23 cells in the prototroch that are arranged in an anterior and posterior tier, with one unpaired cell in the position of 11 o'clock.
source: There are 23 cells in the prototroch that are arranged in an anterior and posterior tier, with one unpaired cell in the position of 11 o'clock (Randel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and citation to previous work.

claim: In the head, there are eight akrotroch cells, six ciliated cells in the nuchal organs, and an unpaired crescent cell.
source: In the head, there are eight akrotroch cells, six ciliated cells in the nuchal organs, and an unpaired crescent cell.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction identifying all multiciliated cells.

claim: The metatroch consists of eight cells.
source: The metatroch consists of eight cells.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction identifying all multiciliated cells.

claim: In the first, second, and third trunk segments there are eight, 14, and 12 paratroch cells, respectively.
source: In the first, second, and third trunk segments there are eight, 14, and 12 paratroch cells, respectively.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction identifying all multiciliated cells.

claim: Eleven cholinergic ciliomotor neurons were identified in the larva.
source: We identified 11 cholinergic ciliomotor neurons in the larva (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and neurotransmitter identification.

claim: The cholinergic ciliomotor neurons include six ventral decussating cholinergic motorneurons (vMNs) and two rhabdomeric photoreceptor cells of the larval eyespots (eyespotPRCR3).
source: These include the previously described six ventral decussating cholinergic motorneurons (vMNs, including MNr1, MNr2, MNr3, MNl1, MNl2, MNl3) and two rhabdomeric photoreceptor cells of the larval eyespots (eyespotPRCR3) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Randel et al., 2014, 2015; Jékely et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and citations to previous work.

claim: Three large biaxonal ciliomotor neurons were found, including a single ciliomotor neuron in the head (MC neuron) and two trunk ciliomotor neurons (Loop neurons).
source: In addition to these neurons, we found three large biaxonal ciliomotor neurons, including a single ciliomotor neuron in the head, the MC neuron, and two trunk ciliomotor neurons that we call the Loop neurons (Figure 2A–D, Video 5).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron morphology.

claim: The MC neuron has its soma in the centre of the larval head and projects two axons that run left and right towards the ciliary band.
source: The MC neuron has its soma in the centre of the larval head and projects two axons that run left and right towards the ciliary band.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron morphology.

claim: The axons of the MC neuron branch at the prototroch and form dorsal and ventral branches that run along the prototroch ring nerve.
source: The axons branch at the prototroch and form dorsal and ventral branches that run along the prototroch ring nerve, a nerve running at the inside of the prototroch ring.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron morphology.

claim: The MC neuron is the most synapse-rich neuron in the entire Platynereis larval connectome.
source: The MC neuron is the most synapse-rich neuron in the entire Platynereis larval connectome (unpublished results) (Randel et al., 2015; Shahidi et al., 2015; Randel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by connectome analysis and citations to previous work.

claim: 341 presynaptic sites were identified in the MC neuron.
source: We identified 341 presynaptic sites in the MC neuron.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and synapse counting.

claim: 335 of the MC neuron's presynaptic sites target the ciliated cells of the prototroch ciliary band.
source: 335 of these target the ciliated cells of the prototroch ciliary band.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and synapse counting.

claim: The MC neuron is the only neuron in the body that is presynaptic to each of the 23 prototroch cells.
source: The MC neuron is the only neuron in the body that is presynaptic to each of the 23 prototroch cells (3–25 synapses per prototroch cell) (Figure 2B,E, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing complete connectivity pattern.

claim: The somas of the Loop neurons are located in the first trunk segment.
source: The somas of the Loop neurons are located in the first trunk segment.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron position.

claim: Loop neurons project one axon anteriorly and one posteriorly.
source: These neurons project one axon anteriorly and one posteriorly (Figure 2C,D, Video 5).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron morphology.

claim: The anterior axon of Loop neurons joins the prototroch ring nerve and continues in the dorsal side of the larva where it runs posteriorly along a thin dorsal nerve.
source: The anterior axon joins the prototroch ring nerve and continues in the dorsal side of the larva where it runs posteriorly along a thin dorsal nerve.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing axon trajectory.

claim: The posterior axon of Loop neurons runs at the lateral edge of the ventral nerve cord, spans all three trunk segments and in the third segment runs to the dorsal side where it turns anteriorly.
source: The posterior axon runs at the lateral edge of the ventral nerve cord, spans all three trunk segments and in the third segment runs to the dorsal side where it turns anteriorly.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing axon trajectory.

claim: The anterior and posterior axons of Loop neurons meet on the dorsal side.
source: The anterior and posterior axons meet on the dorsal side.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing axon trajectory.

claim: The Loop neurons loop around the entire body spanning the head and three segments in both the ventral and dorsal side.
source: The Loop neurons thus loop around the entire body spanning the head and three segments in both the ventral and dorsal side.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing complete neuron morphology.

claim: A single Loop neuron synapses on every ipsilateral paratroch cell, the akrotroch, the ciliated cells of the nuchal organ, and the lateral cells of the prototroch.
source: A single Loop neuron synapses on every ipsilateral paratroch cell, the akrotroch, the ciliated cells of the nuchal organ, and the lateral cells of the prototroch (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The Loop neurons synapse on the crescent cell and represent its only synaptic input.
source: The Loop neurons also synapse on the crescent cell and represent its only synaptic input.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The two Loop neurons innervate all locomotor ciliary fields in the larva, with the exception of the metatroch.
source: Overall, the two Loop neurons innervate all locomotor ciliary fields in the larva, with the exception of the metatroch where we could not find any synaptic input at either side in the reconstructed specimen.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: Only some of the most dorsally and ventrally located prototroch cells (at 5, 6, and 12 o'clock position) lack synaptic input from the Loop neurons.
source: In the prototroch, only some of the most dorsally and ventrally located prototroch cells (at 5, 6, and 12 o'clock position) lack synaptic input from the Loop neurons (Figure 2F, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The ventral cholinergic motorneurons form three left-right pairs.
source: The vMNs form three left-right pairs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron organization.

claim: One pair of ventral motorneurons (MNr1 and MNl1) projects to the ventral nerve chord and innervates ventral paratroch cells and ventral longitudinal muscles.
source: One pair (MNr1 and MNl1) projects to the ventral nerve chord and innervates ventral paratroch cells and ventral longitudinal muscles.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The second pair of ventral motorneurons (MNr2 and MNl2) projects dorsally and posteriorly along the trunk dorsal nerve and innervates lateral prototroch cells, dorsal paratroch cells, and dorsal longitudinal muscles.
source: The second pair (MNr2 and MNl2) projects dorsally and posteriorly along the trunk dorsal nerve and innervates lateral prototroch cells, dorsal paratroch cells, and dorsal longitudinal muscles.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The third pair of ventral motorneurons (MNr3 and MNl3) is a purely ciliomotor pair with no muscle targets.
source: The third pair (MNr3 and MNl3) is a purely ciliomotor pair (no muscle targets).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: Both MNr3 and MNl3 cells synapse on lateral prototroch cells and project to the ventral nerve cord.
source: Both cells synapse on lateral prototroch cells (only the posterior ring) and project to the ventral nerve cord.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The eyespotPRCR3 cells synapse on two ipsilateral prototroch cells of the posterior prototroch belt.
source: The eyespotPRCR3 cells synapse on two ipsilateral prototroch cells of the posterior prototroch belt (Jékely et al., 2008; Randel et al., 2013), representing two of the three direct sensory-ciliomotor neurons in the larva (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (see below).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and citations to previous work.

claim: The cholinergic identity of the ciliomotor neurons is supported by pharmacological experiments and by the expression of cholinergic markers.
source: The cholinergic identity of the above neurons is supported by pharmacological experiments and by the expression of cholinergic markers (Jékely et al., 2008; Randel et al., 2014; Tosches et al., 2014; Denes et al., 2007) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous pharmacological and molecular studies.

claim: A soluble guanylyl cyclase-β gene (sGCβ1) coexpresses with ChAT.
source: We could not obtain a working promoter construct for the canonical cholinergic markers vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) and choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), however, we identified a soluble guanylyl cyclase-β gene (sGCβ1) that coexpresses with ChAT as determined by in situ hybridisation combined with whole-body gene expression registration (Asadulina et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and gene expression registration data.

claim: The Loop neuron was labeled with the sGCβ1 transgenic reporter, confirming its cholinergic identity.
source: In transgenic animals, we could label the Loop neuron (Figure 2G) and the ventral MNl3 neuron (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), as identified by position and morphology, confirming their cholinergic identity.
evidence: Supported by transgenic labeling experiments showing reporter expression.

claim: The MC neuron's cholinergic identity is supported by VAChT expression in the cell body area and by pharmacological evidence.
source: We could not label the MC neuron with this transgene, but its cholinergic identity is supported by VAChT expression in the cell body area of this cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Jékely et al., 2008) and also by pharmacological evidence (see below).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data and citation to previous work, with reference to pharmacological experiments described later.

claim: There are two biaxonal MNant cells that are likely cholinergic.
source: In addition to these 11 cholinergic cells, there are two biaxonal MNant cells, described before (Randel et al., 2015), that are likely cholinergic.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and inference from expression pattern.

claim: The MNant cells have their cell bodies below the ciliary photoreceptor cells in a region of VAChT expression.
source: These cells have their cell bodies below the ciliary photoreceptor cells in a region of VAChT expression, but we could not verify their cholinergic identity at a single-cell resolution.
evidence: Supported by anatomical position and VAChT expression pattern.

claim: The MNant cells form synapses on the contralateral half of the prototroch, the metatroch, and the paratrochs.
source: The MNant cells form synapses on the contralateral half of the prototroch, the metatroch, and the paratrochs (Randel et al., 2015) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and citation to previous work.

claim: Five serotonergic ciliomotor neurons were identified in the larva.
source: We identified five serotonergic ciliomotor neurons in the larva (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and neurotransmitter identification.

claim: There are two serotonergic ciliomotor neurons in the head (Ser-h1), with their somas lateral to the ciliary photoreceptor cells.
source: There are two serotonergic ciliomotor neurons in the head (Ser-h1), with their somas lateral to the ciliary photoreceptor cells (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and immunostaining.

claim: The Ser-h1 neurons cross the midline and project along the contralateral side of the ciliary band, forming several synapses on the ciliated cells.
source: These neurons cross the midline and project along the contralateral side of the ciliary band, forming several synapses on the ciliated cells.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron morphology and connectivity.

claim: The Ser-h1 cells synapse reciprocally on each other in the brain neuropil.
source: The Ser-h1 cells also synapse reciprocally on each other in the brain neuropil.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: There are two large serotonergic biaxonal neurons (Ser-tr1) in the trunk with their somas in the first segment, near the somas of the cholinergic Loop neurons.
source: In the trunk, there are two large serotonergic biaxonal neurons (Ser-tr1) with their somas in the first segment, near the somas of the cholinergic Loop neurons, anterior to the first commissure of the ventral nerve cord (Figure 3D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and immunostaining.

claim: The Ser-tr1 and the Loop neurons represent the largest neurons in the entire Platynereis connectome (between 1,600–1,850 µm total cable length each).
source: The Ser-tr1 and the Loop neurons represent the largest neurons in the entire Platynereis connectome (between 1,600–1,850 µm total cable length each).
evidence: Supported by cable length measurements from connectome reconstruction.

claim: One of the axons of the Ser-tr1 cells projects anteriorly and innervates ipsilateral prototroch cells.
source: One of the axons of the Ser-tr1 cells projects anteriorly and innervates ipsilateral prototroch cells.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron morphology and connectivity.

claim: The other axon of Ser-tr1 cells crosses the midline in the first segment and its axon loops around the body, running in close proximity to the axons of the contralateral Loop neuron.
source: The other axon crosses the midline in the first segment and its axon loops around the body, running in close proximity to the axons of the contralateral Loop neuron.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron morphology.

claim: The Ser-tr1 neurons innervate every paratroch cell as well as the metatroch.
source: The Ser-tr1 neurons also innervate every paratroch cell as well as the metatroch (Figure 3H, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The axons of the Ser-tr1 neurons run parallel to the axons of the Loop neurons throughout the body and are ultrastructurally distinct from the Loop neurons.
source: The axons of the Ser-tr1 neurons run parallel to the axons of the Loop neurons throughout the body and are ultrastructurally distinct from the Loop neurons.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy showing axon ultrastructure.

claim: The Ser-tr1 axons are characterised by a less electron-dense cytoplasm and the lack of dense core vesicles.
source: The Ser-tr1 axons are characterised by a less electron-dense cytoplasm and the lack of dense core vesicles (abundant in the Loop neurons) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy showing axon ultrastructure.

claim: The Ser-tr1 cells were identified as serotonergic by comparing cell body positions and neuron morphologies to cells stained with a serotonin antibody.
source: The Ser-tr1 cells were identified as serotonergic by comparing cell body positions and neuron morphologies to cells stained with a serotonin antibody in 2-day-old and 3-day-old larvae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Fischer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and citation to previous work.

claim: Both the head Ser-h1 neurons and the Ser-tr1 cells could be labeled with a tryptophan hydroxylase (TrpH) transgenic reporter.
source: We also used mosaic transient transgenesis with a construct containing a 5 kB upstream regulatory sequence of the tryptophan hydroxylase gene (TrpH), a marker of serotonergic neurons. We could label both the head Ser-h1 neurons and the Ser-tr1 cells (Figure 3C,F).
evidence: Supported by transgenic labeling experiments showing reporter expression.

claim: A giant serotonergic sensory-motor neuron (pygPBbicil) was identified with a cell body in the pygidium.
source: We also identified a giant serotonergic sensory-motor neuron (pygPBbicil) with a cell body in the pygidium and a unique morphology (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron morphology.

claim: The pygPBbicil neuron has two sensory cilia and two axons that run anterior along the ventral nerve chord.
source: This cell has two sensory cilia and two axons that run anterior along the ventral nerve chord.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron morphology.

claim: The axons of pygPBbicil innervate the prototroch cilia in the head and send a branch to the anterior nervous system.
source: The axons then innervate the prototroch cilia in the head and send a branch to the anterior nervous system.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The pygPBbicil neuron is identifiable by serotonin immunolabeling.
source: The pygPBbicil neuron is identifiable by serotonin immunolabeling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and also expresses the neuropeptide FMRFamide as determined by serial multiplex immunogold (siGOLD) labelling (Shahidi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and citation to previous work.

claim: The pygPBbicil neuron expresses the neuropeptide FMRFamide.
source: The pygPBbicil neuron is identifiable by serotonin immunolabeling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and also expresses the neuropeptide FMRFamide as determined by serial multiplex immunogold (siGOLD) labelling (Shahidi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by siGOLD labeling and citation to previous work.

claim: The pygPBbicil neuron, together with the eyespot photoreceptor cells, is the third sensory neuron that directly synapses on ciliated cells.
source: This cell, together with the eyespot photoreceptor cells, is the third sensory neuron that directly synapses on ciliated cells.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: There are three molecularly distinct, asymmetric peptidergic cells (cMNvl, cMNd, cMNATO) with their cell bodies at the level of the prototroch ciliary band.
source: There are three molecularly distinct, asymmetric peptidergic cells (cMNvl, cMNd, cMNATO) with their cell bodies at the level of the prototroch ciliary band (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and molecular characterization.

claim: The two ventral-lateral cells (cMNvl, cMNATO) express tyrosine hydroxylase, a marker of dopaminergic neurons.
source: The two ventral-lateral cells (cMNvl, cMNATO) express tyrosine hydroxylase, a marker of dopaminergic neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization showing gene expression.

claim: The cMNATO cell expresses dopamine-β-hydroxylase, indicating that it is noradrenergic.
source: The cMNATO cell also expresses dopamine-β-hydroxylase, indicating that it is noradrenergic (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization showing gene expression and inference about neurotransmitter identity.

claim: The neurons cMNvl and cMNd express pigment dispersing factor (PDF).
source: The neurons cMNvl and cMNd express pigment dispersing factor (PDF), as determined by siGOLD (Shahidi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by siGOLD labeling and citation to previous work.

claim: The cMNATO cell expresses allatotropin.
source: The cMNATO cell expresses allatotropin and its full morphology is revealed by immunostaining with an allatotropin antibody (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing neuropeptide expression.

claim: The cMNvl neuron expresses FLamide and FVamide neuropeptides.
source: The cMNvl neuron also expresses FLamide and FVamide, cMNATO expresses DLamide, and cMNd expresses the neuropeptides L11, and LYamide, as revealed by immunostainings (Conzelmann et al., 2011) and in situ hybridisation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining, in situ hybridization, and citation to previous work.

claim: The cMNATO neuron expresses DLamide neuropeptide.
source: The cMNvl neuron also expresses FLamide and FVamide, cMNATO expresses DLamide, and cMNd expresses the neuropeptides L11, and LYamide, as revealed by immunostainings (Conzelmann et al., 2011) and in situ hybridisation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining, in situ hybridization, and citation to previous work.

claim: The cMNd neuron expresses the neuropeptides L11 and LYamide.
source: The cMNvl neuron also expresses FLamide and FVamide, cMNATO expresses DLamide, and cMNd expresses the neuropeptides L11, and LYamide, as revealed by immunostainings (Conzelmann et al., 2011) and in situ hybridisation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining, in situ hybridization, and citation to previous work.

claim: The cMN cells synapse on prototroch cells and the MC cell and also synapse reciprocally among themselves.
source: The cMN cells synapse on prototroch cells and the MC cell and also synapse reciprocally among themselves (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The network of ciliomotor neurons and multiciliated cells can be subdivided into three communities based on modularity analysis.
source: To analyse the overall connectivity of the ciliomotor system (Video 8, Supplementary file 1), we next performed modularity analysis to identify more strongly connected communities of cells (Blondel et al., 2008). We could subdivide the network of ciliomotor neurons and multiciliated cells into three communities each containing cells that were more strongly connected among each other (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by network analysis of connectome data and citation to analysis method.

claim: Module 1 includes ciliomotor neurons that only innervate prototroch cells.
source: Module 1 includes ciliomotor neurons that only innervate prototroch cells (MC, cMN, Ser-h1, and pygPBbicil, MNl3, MNr3, eyespotPRCR3, and most prototroch cells).
evidence: Supported by modularity analysis of connectivity data.

claim: Module 2 is composed of neurons that share ciliated target cells primarily on the right body side.
source: Module 2 is composed of the right (ipsilaterally-projecting) Loopr neuron and the left (contralaterally projecting) Ser-tr1l, MNantl, MNl1, and MNl2 neurons. These neurons share ciliated target cells that are primarily on the right body side (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by modularity analysis of connectivity data.

claim: Module 3 includes neurons providing innervation primarily to cilia on the left body side.
source: Module 3 includes neurons providing innervation primarily to cilia on the left body side (Loopl, Ser-tr1r, MNantr, MNr1, and MNr2).
evidence: Supported by modularity analysis of connectivity data.

claim: The cMN neurons are presynaptic to the MC neuron, the MNant and the Loop neurons.
source: The cMN neurons are presynaptic to the MC neuron, the MNant and the Loop neurons, and show reciprocal connectivity with the Ser-h1 and pygPBbicil cells.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The cMN neurons show reciprocal connectivity with the Ser-h1 and pygPBbicil cells.
source: The cMN neurons are presynaptic to the MC neuron, the MNant and the Loop neurons, and show reciprocal connectivity with the Ser-h1 and pygPBbicil cells.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The Ser-h1 cells are presynaptic to the MC neuron.
source: The Ser-h1 cells are presynaptic to the MC neuron and the Ser-tr1 and Loop neurons are reciprocally connected.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The Ser-tr1 and Loop neurons are reciprocally connected.
source: The Ser-h1 cells are presynaptic to the MC neuron and the Ser-tr1 and Loop neurons are reciprocally connected.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The pygPBbicil neuron is presynaptic to the MC cell.
source: The pygPBbicil neuron is also presynaptic to the MC cell (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity pattern.

claim: The cMN neurons display spontaneous rhythmic activity patterns.
source: Calcium imaging revealed that the cMN neurons display spontaneous rhythmic activity patterns.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments showing periodic activity.

claim: The cMNvl and cMNd neurons showed rhythmic increases in the GCaMP signal in synchrony with the ciliary band.
source: We found that the cMNvl and cMNd neurons showed rhythmic increases in the GCaMP signal in synchrony with the ciliary band (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments showing correlated activity.

claim: The activity of the cMNATO was negatively correlated with the two other cMN neurons and the ciliary band.
source: In contrast, the activity of the cMNATO was negatively correlated with the two other cMN neurons and the ciliary band (Figure 6C,D,F, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments showing anti-correlated activity.

claim: The rhythmic activation of the cMN neurons could be detected in larvae from 24 hr-post-fertilisation onwards.
source: We could detect the rhythmic activation of the cMN neurons in larvae from 24 hr-post-fertilisation (hpf) onwards.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments at different developmental stages.

claim: The MC neuron could be identified based on its position and biaxonal morphology as revealed by the GCaMP signal.
source: We could identify the MC neuron based on its position and biaxonal morphology as revealed by the GCaMP signal (Video 9).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing neuron morphology.

claim: The activity of the MC neuron was periodic and strongly correlated with the activity of the prototroch cells and with ciliary arrests.
source: We found that the activity of the MC neuron was periodic and strongly correlated with the activity of the prototroch cells and with ciliary arrests (Figure 7A,D, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments showing correlated activity.

claim: The median cycle length of the periodic activation of the MC neuron was 71 s.
source: Recording from 96 different larvae (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1) followed by Fourier analysis of the calcium signals revealed a median cycle length of 71 s of the periodic activation of the MC neuron.
evidence: Supported by Fourier analysis of calcium imaging data from multiple larvae.

claim: In 43% of larvae the MC neuron had a cycle length between 50–100 s.
source: In 43% of larvae the MC neuron had a cycle length between 50–100 s (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by frequency distribution analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: Two cells in the first segment were activated synchronously with the ciliary band cells and could be identified as the Loop neurons.
source: In the trunk, we also identified two cells in the first segment that were activated synchronously with the ciliary band cells and thus the MC neuron (though not imaged simultaneously for technical reasons). These two trunk cells had somas in the approximate position of the two Loop neurons with ipsilaterally projecting axons, and could thus be identified as the Loop neurons (Figure 7B,D, see also Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing activity pattern and cell position matching connectome data.

claim: MC-cell ablation eliminated the rhythmic activity in the prototroch cells and thus most ciliary arrests.
source: MC-cell ablation eliminated the rhythmic activity in the prototroch cells and thus most ciliary arrests (Figure 7E,F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by laser ablation experiments showing loss of rhythmic activity.

claim: The MC cell is essential for triggering the rhythmic arrests of the prototroch cilia.
source: This shows that the MC cell is essential for triggering the rhythmic arrests of the prototroch cilia.
evidence: Inferred from ablation experiments showing loss of arrests after MC cell ablation.

claim: When larvae were treated with alpha-bungarotoxin, the MC neuron continued to rhythmically activate while calcium signals progressively reduced and then disappeared in the ciliary band.
source: When we imaged alpha-bungarotoxin-treated larvae, we observed the decoupling of the activity of the MC neuron and the ciliary band. While the MC neuron continued to rhythmically activate, the calcium signals were progressively reduced and then disappeared in the ciliary band (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments with calcium imaging.

claim: Alpha-bungarotoxin treatment eliminated ciliary arrests.
source: Ciliary arrests were also eliminated (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments observing ciliary behavior.

claim: Cholinergic signalling is not required for the generation of the neuronal rhythm but is required for ciliary arrests.
source: This indicates that cholinergic signalling is not required for the generation of the neuronal rhythm but is required for ciliary arrests.
evidence: Inferred from pharmacological experiments showing continued MC neuron activity but loss of ciliary arrests after blocking cholinergic transmission.

claim: The ventral cholinergic motorneurons were previously shown to rhythmically activate and were suggested to trigger ciliary arrests.
source: The ventral cholinergic motorneurons (vMN) were previously shown to rhythmically activate, and were suggested to trigger ciliary arrests (Tosches et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Three ventral MN cells were identified that were activated either synchronously or asynchronously with the ciliary band.
source: We could identify three ventral MN cells that were activated either synchronously or asynchronously (designated vMNsync and vMNasync) with the ciliary band (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments showing activity patterns.

claim: Following MC neuron ablation, the activity of the prototroch correlated with the activity of the vMNsync neuron suggesting that this cholinergic neuron can maintain a lower rate of prototroch activation.
source: Following MC neuron ablation, the activity of the prototroch correlated with the activity of the vMNsync neuron suggesting that this cholinergic neuron can maintain a lower rate of prototroch activation.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging after ablation experiments and inference about neuron function.

claim: The head serotonergic cells (Ser-h1) showed anti-correlated activity with the ciliated cells and the MC neuron.
source: Correlation analysis of the calcium-imaging videos revealed that the head serotonergic cells (Ser-h1), identified by position and morphology, showed anti-correlated activity with the ciliated cells and the MC neuron (Figure 8A,B,E, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: Two neurons in the ventral nerve cord whose activity was anti-correlated with the activity of the ciliary band were identified, with cell-body positions corresponding to the position of the Ser-tr1 cells.
source: In the ventral nerve cord, we also identified two neurons whose activity was anti-correlated with the activity of the ciliary band. (Figure 8C–E). The GCaMP signal did not reveal the axonal morphology of these neurons, but their cell-body position corresponded to the position of the Ser-tr1 cells.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing activity pattern and cell position.

claim: Photoactivation experiments confirmed the identity of the Ser-tr1 neurons by labeling serotonergic cells.
source: To directly test the identity of these cells, we performed in vivo photoactivation experiments. We co-injected GCaMP mRNA with an mRNA encoding a photoactivatable mCherry fluorescent protein (PAmCherry1). During calcium imaging, we identified the Ser-tr1 candidate neuron based on its activity and then photoactivated PAmCherry1 in this neuron. The larvae were subsequently fixed and stained for serotonin. In all cases (n = 11 larvae) we labelled the serotonergic Ser-tr1 neuron, together with a few out-of-focus cells that were labelled more weakly (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by photoactivation experiments combined with immunostaining.

claim: Serotonin increased ciliary beat frequency compared to untreated larvae.
source: Serotonin increased ciliary beat frequency and inhibited ciliary arrests compared to untreated larvae (Figure 8F,G, Figure 8—source data 2, Figure 8—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments measuring ciliary beat frequency.

claim: Serotonin inhibited ciliary arrests compared to untreated larvae.
source: Serotonin increased ciliary beat frequency and inhibited ciliary arrests compared to untreated larvae (Figure 8F,G, Figure 8—source data 2, Figure 8—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments measuring ciliary arrests.

claim: The ciliomotor system represents a novel pacemaker motor circuit that forms a stop-and-go system for ciliary swimming.
source: The ciliomotor system we describe here represents a novel pacemaker motor circuit that forms a stop-and-go system for ciliary swimming (Figure 9).
evidence: Inferred from the combined connectome, activity, and functional data showing alternating phases of activity.

claim: Some of the neurons in the ciliomotor circuit (Loop and Ser-tr1 neurons) span twice the entire body length to coordinately regulate segmental cilia.
source: Remarkably, some of the neurons in this circuit (Loop and Ser-tr1 neurons) span twice the entire body length to coordinately regulate segmental cilia.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron morphology.

claim: Many ciliomotor neurons have a biaxonal morphology, a feature that is very rare in Platynereis neurons belonging to other circuits.
source: Furthermore, many cells have a biaxonal morphology, a feature that is very rare in Platynereis neurons belonging to other circuits (Randel et al., 2014; Shahidi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and citations to previous work on other circuits.

claim: Serotonergic neurons innervating ciliary bands have been described in several groups, including annelid, mollusc, phoronid, and bryozoan larvae, and likely represent an ancestral character in lophotrochozoans.
source: Serotonergic neurons innervating ciliary bands have been described in several groups (Hay-Schmidt, 2000), including annelid (Voronezhskaya et al., 2003), mollusc (Friedrich et al., 2002; Kempf et al., 1997), phoronid (Temereva and Wanninger, 2012), and bryozoan larvae (Wanninger et al., 2005), and likely represent an ancestral character in lophotrochozoans (Wanninger et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to comparative morphological studies and inference about evolutionary history.

claim: Serotonergic innervation of ciliary bands is present in deuterostomes, including echinoderm and hemichordate larvae.
source: Serotonergic innervation of ciliary bands is also present in deuterostomes, including echinoderm and hemichordate larvae (Hay-Schmidt, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to comparative morphological studies.

claim: Catecholamine-containing processes innervate ciliary bands in mollusc, phoronid, echinoderm, hemichordate, and nemertean larvae.
source: Likewise, catecholamine-containing processes innervate ciliary bands in mollusc (Croll et al., 1997), phoronid (Hay-Schmidt, 1990b), echinoderm, hemichordate (Dautov and Nezlin, 1992; Nezlin, 2000), and nemertean larvae (Hay-Schmidt, 1990a).
evidence: Supported by citations to comparative morphological studies.

claim: Cholinergic nerves associate with ciliary bands in echinoderm, hemichordate, and mollusc larvae.
source: Cholinergic nerves also often associate with ciliary bands in echinoderm, hemichordate (Dautov and Nezlin, 1992; Nezlin, 2000), and mollusc larvae (Raineri, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to comparative morphological studies.

claim: One intriguing scenario is that ciliated larvae and their nervous systems, including the apical sensory organ and the ciliomotor systems, are homologous across bilaterians or even eumetazoans.
source: One intriguing (although controversial) scenario is that ciliated larvae and their nervous systems, including the apical sensory organ (Marlow et al., 2014) and the ciliomotor systems, are homologous across bilaterians or even eumetazoans.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about evolutionary relationships, with citation to previous work.

claim: The Platynereis ciliomotor system may represent an ancient system that evolved close to the origin of the nervous system.
source: If this is the case, this could mean that the Platynereis ciliomotor system represents an ancient system that evolved close to the origin of the nervous system (Jékely, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis conditional on the homology scenario, with citation to previous work.

claim: The internal coordination of multiciliated surfaces may have been one of the early functions of nervous systems.
source: The internal coordination of multiciliated surfaces may thus have been one of the early functions of nervous systems (Jékely et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about early nervous system function, with citation to previous work.

claim: Multiciliated surfaces harboring synchronously beating cilia can generate fluid flow or drive locomotion.
source: Ciliated surfaces harbouring synchronously beating cilia can generate fluid flow or drive locomotion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ciliated surfaces.

claim: In ciliary swimmers, ciliary beating, arrests, and changes in beat frequency are often coordinated across extended or discontinuous surfaces.
source: In ciliary swimmers, ciliary beating, arrests, and changes in beat frequency are often coordinated across extended or discontinuous surfaces.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ciliary coordination in swimmers.

claim: Multiciliated surfaces can effectively generate flow in many different contexts, including driving solute transport in reef corals, moving mucus and particles in mucociliary epithelia, driving the cerebrospinal fluid, or moving the ovum in the mammalian oviduct.
source: Such surfaces can effectively generate flow in many different contexts, including the driving of solute transport in reef corals (Shapiro et al., 2014), moving mucus and particles in mucociliary epithelia (Kramer-Zucker et al., 2005; Walentek et al., 2014), driving the cerebrospinal fluid (Faubel et al., 2016), or moving the ovum in the mammalian oviduct (Halbert et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on various ciliated systems.

claim: Multiciliated surfaces can drive locomotion, as in ciliates, colonial green algae, or marine invertebrate larvae.
source: Multiciliated surfaces can also drive locomotion, as in ciliates, colonial green algae, or marine invertebrate larvae (Tamm, 1972; Chia et al., 1984; Brumley et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on ciliary locomotion.

claim: A universal feature of multiciliated surfaces is the long-range beat synchronisation of individual cilia into metachronal waves.
source: A universal feature of multiciliated surfaces is the long-range beat synchronisation of individual cilia into metachronal waves (Tamm, 1984; Brumley et al., 2012; Knight-Jones, 1954; Tamm, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on ciliary synchronization.

claim: Theoretical studies indicate that metachronal waves are energetically efficient and have a higher efficiency of flow generation than non-metachronal beating.
source: Theoretical studies indicate that metachronal waves are energetically efficient and have a higher efficiency of flow generation than non-metachronal beating (Osterman and Vilfan, 2011; Gueron and Levit-Gurevich, 1999; Elgeti and Gompper, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical modeling studies.

claim: Metachronal coordination requires the orientation of ciliary beating planes during development.
source: Metachronal coordination requires the orientation of ciliary beating planes during development (Mitchell et al., 2007; Park et al., 2008; Mitchell et al., 2009; Guirao et al., 2010; Vladar et al., 2012; Kunimoto et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous developmental studies.

claim: If cilia are oriented, synchronisation emerges by hydrodynamic coupling as adjacent cilia engage by flow.
source: If cilia are oriented, synchronisation emerges by hydrodynamic coupling as adjacent cilia engage by flow (Brumley et al., 2014; Elgeti and Gompper, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous biophysical studies.

claim: Basal body coupling can also contribute to beat synchronisation as demonstrated in green algae.
source: In addition, basal body coupling can also contribute to beat synchronisation as demonstrated in green algae (Wan and Goldstein, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on green algae.

claim: Biophysical mechanisms alone cannot explain all aspects of ciliary beat synchronisation.
source: However, biophysical mechanisms alone cannot explain all aspects of ciliary beat synchronisation.
evidence: This is an inference based on examples of regulation that cannot be explained by biophysics alone.

claim: The flow-networks generated by ependymal cilia show complex reorganisation that is under circadian regulation.
source: For example, the flow-networks generated by ependymal cilia show complex reorganisation that is under circadian regulation (Faubel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on ependymal cilia.

claim: In mucociliary surfaces, changes in ciliary beat frequency are coordinated to regulate flow rates.
source: In mucociliary surfaces, changes in ciliary beat frequency are coordinated to regulate flow rates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mucociliary regulation.

claim: Some changes in ciliary beat frequency in mucociliary surfaces are due to locally secreted diffusible molecules, including serotonin and neuropeptides.
source: Some of these changes are due to locally secreted diffusible molecules, including serotonin (Maruyama et al., 1984; König et al., 2009; Walentek et al., 2014) and neuropeptides (Conductier et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on neuromodulation of cilia.

claim: Long-range ciliary coordination is often under neuronal control.
source: However, long-range ciliary coordination is often under neuronal control (Doran et al., 2004; Tamm, 2014; Arkett et al., 1987; Kuang and Goldberg, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on neuronal control of cilia.

claim: In the ctenophore Pleurobrachia, prey-capture triggers a rapid synchronised beating of all eight ciliary comb-rows resulting in fast forward swimming.
source: In the ctenophore Pleurobrachia, prey-capture triggers a rapid synchronised beating of all eight ciliary comb-rows resulting in fast forward swimming (Tamm, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on ctenophore behavior.

claim: In gastropod veliger larvae, the normal beating of velar cilia is periodically interrupted by coordinated, velum-wide ciliary arrests, triggered by calcium-spikes.
source: In gastropod veliger larvae, the normal beating of velar cilia is periodically interrupted by coordinated, velum-wide ciliary arrests, triggered by calcium-spikes (Arkett et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on gastropod larvae.

claim: Annelid larvae show regular and coordinated arrests of the entire prototroch ciliary band.
source: Similarly, annelid larvae show regular and coordinated arrests of the entire prototroch ciliary band (Conzelmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on annelid larvae.

claim: Coordinated changes in ciliary activity, often triggered throughout the whole body, require neuronal control.
source: Such coordinated changes in ciliary activity, often triggered throughout the whole body, require neuronal control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complexity and coordination of ciliary responses.

claim: The neuronal circuits coordinating whole-body ciliary activity have not been described in any animal prior to this study.
source: The neuronal circuits coordinating whole-body ciliary activity have not been described in any animal.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Platynereis has emerged as a powerful model to study neural cell types and development and the whole-body circuit bases of larval behaviour.
source: Platynereis has emerged as a powerful model to study neural cell types and development (Tomer et al., 2010; Marlow et al., 2014; Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007) and the whole-body circuit bases of larval behaviour, including conical-scanning and visual phototaxis (Jékely et al., 2008; Randel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work establishing Platynereis as a model system.

claim: Platynereis nectochaete larvae have three trunk segments and use segmentally arranged ciliary bands to swim and muscles to turn while swimming or to crawl on the substrate.
source: Platynereis nectochaete larvae (Fischer et al., 2010) have three trunk segments and use segmentally arranged ciliary bands to swim and muscles to turn while swimming (Randel et al., 2014) or to crawl on the substrate.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on larval anatomy and behavior.

claim: Ciliary beating in Platynereis is under neuromodulatory control and can be influenced by several neuropeptides and melatonin.
source: Ciliary beating is also under neuromodulatory control and can be influenced by several neuropeptides and melatonin (Conzelmann et al., 2011; Tosches et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on neuromodulation.

claim: The ciliomotor circuitry constitutes a stop-and-go pacemaker system for the whole-body coordination of ciliary locomotion.
source: The ciliomotor circuitry thus constitutes a stop-and-go pacemaker system for the whole-body coordination of ciliary locomotion.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the connectome, activity, and functional data presented.

claim: The synchronous rhythmic activation of cholinergic cells drives the coordinated arrests of all cilia.
source: The synchronous rhythmic activation of cholinergic cells drives the coordinated arrests of all cilia.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging and ablation experiments showing correlation and necessity.

claim: The serotonergic cells are active when cilia are beating.
source: The serotonergic cells are active when cilia are beating.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing anti-correlated activity with arrests.

claim: Serotonin inhibits the cholinergic rhythm, and increases ciliary beat frequency.
source: Serotonin inhibits the cholinergic rhythm, and increases ciliary beat frequency.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing effects of serotonin application.

claim: Based on their connectivity and alternating activity, the catecholaminergic cells may generate the rhythm.
source: Based on their connectivity and alternating activity, the catecholaminergic cells may generate the rhythm.
evidence: This is an inference based on connectivity patterns and activity correlations.

claim: The connectome and imaging data indicate the rhythm is generated by the interactions of the ciliomotor neurons themselves.
source: Our connectome and imaging data indicate the rhythm is generated by the interactions of the ciliomotor neurons themselves.
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectivity and activity patterns observed.

claim: The presence of many and often reciprocal synaptic connections between the ciliomotor motorneurons supports that the rhythm is generated by the interactions of the ciliomotor neurons themselves.
source: This is supported by the presence of many and often reciprocal synaptic connections between the ciliomotor motorneurons.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity patterns.

claim: Together with the MC neuron, the cMN cells are the first neurons that show a rhythmic pattern during development.
source: First, together with the MC neuron, the cMN cells are the first neurons that show a rhythmic pattern during development.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging at different developmental stages.

claim: The cMN neurons contain three cells with distinct transmitter profiles suggesting the possibility of antagonistic reciprocal signalling.
source: Second, they contain three cells with distinct transmitter profiles suggesting the possibility of antagonistic reciprocal signalling.
evidence: Supported by molecular characterization and inference about signaling mechanisms.

claim: The cMN neurons are presynaptic or reciprocally connected with all the other ciliomotor neurons.
source: Third, they are presynaptic or reciprocally connected with all the other ciliomotor neurons.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity patterns.

claim: The cMN neurons are presynaptic to both the MC and the Loop neurons that are themselves only weakly connected, yet activate synchronously.
source: For example, the cMN neurons are presynaptic to both the MC and the Loop neurons that are themselves only weakly connected, yet activate synchronously.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and calcium imaging data.

claim: Blocking cholinergic transmission did not eliminate the rhythmic activation of the MC neuron, excluding a role for cholinergic neurons in rhythm generation.
source: We can also exclude a role for cholinergic neurons in rhythm generation since blocking cholinergic transmission did not eliminate the rhythmic activation of the MC neuron.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing continued MC neuron activity after blocking cholinergic transmission.

claim: The MC neuron together with the two Loop neurons is able to trigger coordinated, body-wide ciliary arrests.
source: Our imaging and connectome data suggest that the MC neuron together with the two Loop neurons is able to trigger coordinated, body-wide ciliary arrests.
evidence: This is an inference based on connectivity patterns, activity correlations, and ablation experiments.

claim: These three cells (MC and two Loop neurons) innervate all multiciliated cells in the body with the exception of the metatroch.
source: These three cells innervate all multiciliated cells in the body (with the exception of the metatroch).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity patterns.

claim: Arrests of metatroch cilia may be triggered by the MNant neurons, the only putatively cholinergic neurons that innervate the metatroch.
source: Arrests of metatroch cilia may be triggered by the MNant neurons, the only putatively cholinergic neurons that innervate the metatroch.
evidence: This is an inference based on connectivity patterns.

claim: The metatroch is a special ciliary band that in some feeding trochophore larvae beats in opposition to the prototroch to collect food particles.
source: The metatroch is a special ciliary band that in some feeding trochophore larvae beats in opposition to the prototroch to collect food particles (Rouse, 1999; Pernet and Strathmann, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on metatroch function.

claim: The distinct pattern of innervation for the metatroch may reflect the unique evolutionary history of this ciliary band.
source: The distinct pattern of innervation for the metatroch may reflect the unique evolutionary history of this ciliary band.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary history based on innervation patterns.

claim: The only synaptic contacts to the crescent cell come from the Loop neurons.
source: The only synaptic contacts to the crescent cell come from the Loop neurons.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity patterns.

claim: Crescent cilia respond differently to stimulation than locomotor cilia and start beating instead of arresting.
source: However, crescent cilia respond differently to stimulation than locomotor cilia and start beating instead of arresting.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing distinct behavior of crescent cilia.

claim: Beating of the crescent cilia may serve to generate water flow to facilitate chemosensory sampling in the apical organ, similar to the role of cilia-generated flows in olfaction in fish.
source: Beating of the crescent cilia may serve to generate water flow to facilitate chemosensory sampling in the apical organ, similar to the role of cilia-generated flows in olfaction in fish (Reiten et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about function based on location and behavior, with citation to analogous system.

claim: Four serotonergic ciliomotor neurons collectively innervate all ciliary bands.
source: Parallel and upstream to the cholinergic system, we identified four serotonergic ciliomotor neurons that also collectively innervate all ciliary bands.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing connectivity patterns.

claim: Serotonergic cells are presynaptic to the cholinergic cells.
source: Serotonergic cells are also presynaptic to the cholinergic cells and serotonin application suppresses closures and increases ciliary beat frequency.
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction and pharmacological experiments.

claim: Serotonin application suppresses closures and increases ciliary beat frequency.
source: Serotonergic cells are also presynaptic to the cholinergic cells and serotonin application suppresses closures and increases ciliary beat frequency.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments.

claim: One possibility is that serotonin influences the pacemaker activity thereby indirectly affecting closures.
source: One possibility is that serotonin influences the pacemaker activity thereby indirectly affecting closures.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of serotonin action.

claim: Serotonin may act directly on ciliated cells via serotonergic synapses to increase beat frequency.
source: Serotonin may also act directly on ciliated cells via serotonergic synapses to increase beat frequency.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of serotonin action.

claim: The activation of the serotonergic cells corresponds to periods of swimming.
source: The activation of the serotonergic cells corresponds to periods of swimming and thus these cells are likely responsible for the resumption of beating.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing activity patterns and inference about function.

claim: The serotonergic cells are likely responsible for the resumption of beating.
source: The activation of the serotonergic cells corresponds to periods of swimming and thus these cells are likely responsible for the resumption of beating.
evidence: This is an inference based on activity patterns and pharmacological effects.

claim: The monoamines and neuropeptides mapped to the ciliomotor neurons may act at synapses or extrasynaptically.
source: The monoamines and neuropeptides we mapped to the ciliomotor neurons may act at synapses or extrasynaptically (Bentley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about signaling mechanisms with citation to previous work.

claim: In freely-swimming Platynereis larvae the alternation of periods of upward swimming (when cilia beat) and sinking (when cilia are arrested) is important for maintaining a constant depth in the water column of the negatively buoyant larvae.
source: It was shown that in freely-swimming Platynereis larvae the alternation of periods of upward swimming (when cilia beat) and sinking (when cilia are arrested) is important for maintaining a constant depth in the water column of the negatively buoyant larvae (Conzelmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous behavioral study.

claim: The Platynereis larval nervous system exhibits a rhythmic autonomic activity already in the 1-day-old stage, when the nervous system only consists of <20 differentiated neurons.
source: It is remarkable that the Platynereis larval nervous system exhibits a rhythmic autonomic activity already in the 1-day-old stage, when the nervous system only consists of <20 differentiated neurons.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging at early developmental stages.

claim: The ongoing rhythmic activity in Platynereis larvae is present in all larvae and is not induced by sensory input.
source: This ongoing activity is present in all larvae and is not induced by sensory input.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing spontaneous activity in immobilized larvae.

claim: Early larval behaviour in Platynereis is best described in operant terms.
source: Early larval behaviour is thus best described in operant terms (Brembs, 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of behavior with citation to conceptual framework.

claim: Several neuromodulators, including neuropeptides and melatonin were shown to either inhibit or induce ciliary arrests, and thereby shift larvae upwards or downwards in the water column.
source: Several neuromodulators, including neuropeptides and melatonin were shown to either inhibit or induce ciliary arrests, and thereby shift larvae upwards or downwards in the water column (Conzelmann et al., 2011, 2013; Tosches et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous pharmacological studies.

claim: Many neuropeptides are expressed in sensory-neurosecretory cells, suggesting that sensory cues can influence larval swimming by neuroendocrine signalling.
source: Many neuropeptides are expressed in sensory-neurosecretory cells, suggesting that sensory cues can influence larval swimming by neuroendocrine signalling (Conzelmann et al., 2013; Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on neuropeptide expression and inference about signaling mechanisms.

claim: Many ciliomotor neurons have a biaxonal morphology.
source: Furthermore, many cells have a biaxonal morphology, a feature that is very rare in Platynereis neurons belonging to other circuits (Randel et al., 2014; Shahidi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by connectome reconstruction showing neuron morphology.

claim: Comparative morphological studies using histological techniques suggest that similar ciliomotor systems, sometimes with large biaxonal neurons, are widespread in ciliated larvae.
source: Comparative morphological studies using histological techniques suggest that similar ciliomotor systems, sometimes with large biaxonal neurons (Temereva and Wanninger, 2012), are widespread in ciliated larvae.
evidence: Supported by citation to comparative morphological study.
